summary: GEONOVA is an interactive science website and presentation that identifies and characterizes seven Earth locations as analogs for the Moon and Mars. Devon Island, Bodélé Depression, McMurdo Dry Valleys and Lanzarote serve Mars. Harrat Rahat, Dallol and Jebel Uweinat serve the Moon. For each site, we explain what makes it analogous, where the analogy breaks down, and how it can help prepare real missions. This matters because testing equipment, procedures and science on Earth first reduces risk and cost before exploring the Moon and Mars.
details:
GEONOVA is an interactive science website and a 7-slide presentation that identifies and characterizes seven Earth locations as analogs for the Moon and Mars. We compared each site’s geology, terrain, climate extremes, ice and permafrost, dust and wind processes, and subsurface features, and we explain what matches and where the analogy breaks down.

Mars analogs: Devon Island (polar impact crater on ice-rich permafrost), Bodélé Depression (wind-carved ridges, the dustiest place on Earth), McMurdo Dry Valleys (dry permafrost linked to the Phoenix landing site) and Lanzarote (La Corona lava tube, rover tests). Moon analogs: Harrat Rahat (basaltic volcanic field), Dallol (volcanic heat under a very dry salt plain) and Jebel Uweinat (rocky, dry massif). Lanzarote’s basalts also became the LZS-1 lunar soil simulant.

The website (Home, Explore, Missions, Learn, Search) lets visitors explore space themselves. It helps planners choose the right place to test technology, train crews and rovers, and study resources and habitability, reducing risk and cost before real missions.

We went beyond visual similarity and stated Earth’s limits: it cannot reproduce reduced gravity, the lunar vacuum, the thin Martian atmosphere or radiation.

Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Cloudflare Workers, Canva, Python.

SI use: Claude (Anthropic) was used to organize our research into slides and polish the text(slides only)
